title: SRE: SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, Reliability Initiatives, and Runbook Standards
author: Ari Chen
summary: Standards and best practices for SRE documentation at Redwood Inference: SLO definitions and ownership, error budget policies, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review standards, operational tooling, and runbook requirements.
content:
Overview

This page describes Redwood Inference's SRE documentation standards and the required artefacts for services that are in production. It consolidates SLO and error budget practices, capacity planning templates, reliability initiatives, incident review expectations, operational tooling requirements, and runbook structure. The goal is consistent, auditable, and actionable SRE documentation across teams.

1) SLO and Error Budget Standards

Intro: Every customer-facing service and internal platform (critical infra, control plane, billing, serving runtime) must define at least one availability SLO and one latency or correctness SLO where applicable. SLOs must be actionable and owned.

Required metadata for each SLO
- service_name: short identifier (e.g., runtime-token-service)
- owner: primary oncall/rotation (team + pager alias)
- objective: percentage target (e.g., 99.9%)
- window: rolling window used (30d / 90d)
- measurement: concrete metric (e.g., requests_p99_latency_ms, successful_response_rate)
- detection_query: link to metric/alert query (Prometheus, Datadog, etc.)
- error_budget_policy: escalation and rate-limit policy when budget is exhausted

SLO examples (table style)
| SLO name | Metric | Objective | Window | Owner | Error budget action |
| runtime-api-availability | request_success_rate | 99.95% | 30d | eng-serving-runtime-oncall | auto-roll back canary, notify execs at 50% burn |
| prompt-routing-latency-95 | request_latency_ms_p95 | < 1200ms | 30d | infra-routing-team | migrate traffic to low-latency pool when > 20% over target |

Error budget policy template (required)
1. Define burn rate thresholds:
   - low (0-25% of budget used): monitor, no action
   - medium (25-50%): notify service owner and SRE lead, begin exec review if trend continues
   - high (50-100%): freeze risky changes, scale-up capacity or rollback recent deploys, engage oncall
   - exhausted (>100%): mandatory incident review within 24 hours, prioritize remediation roadmap, adjust SLIs/SLOs only via ADR
2. Specify automated mitigations where possible (traffic shifting, fallback models, reduced throughput mode).
3. Document customer-facing comms requirements for prolonged budget burn.

2) Capacity Planning Standards

Purpose: Ensure predictable capacity for hosted, dedicated, and private deployments. Capacity docs must support the following: baseline sizing, burst capacity strategy, autoscaling policies, and cost trade-offs.

Required sections in a capacity plan
- service_overview: short description and traffic patterns
- critical_slo_dependencies: list SLOs that depend on capacity decisions
- baseline_rps: measured baseline requests per second and P95 load profile
- peak_rps: expected peak during business-critical events and burst scenarios
- headroom_policy: required headroom (e.g., 30% for sudden spikes, 50% for launch)
- autoscaling_policy: metrics, cooldowns, min/max instances, and scaling step sizes
- failure_modes_and_mitigation: expected failures and runbook pointers
- cost_estimate: monthly costs for baseline and peak configurations

Capacity checklist (must be included for each quarterly review)
- load tests executed (link to artifacts)
- model sequence-length distribution profile (for inference services)
- GPU memory / KV cache sizing and hot-shard analysis
- traffic locality and region failover plan

3) Runbook and Operational Playbook Standards

Runbook purpose: provide an oncall responder with a concise, prioritized set of steps to restore service and mitigate customer impact. Each runbook must be a single-page quick-reference plus a longer postmortem guide where needed.

Runbook required sections
- runbook_id: unique short name
- status_page_row: boolean (is this reflected on the public status page?)
- severity_triage: mapping from symptom to suggested initial severity
- quick_checks: immediate queries to run (prometheus/datadog queries, kubectl commands, sql checks)
- mitigation_steps: ordered step-by-step actions (1, 2, 3) including CLI commands and safe rollbacks
- escalation: who to call at each step (pager aliases, Slack channel)
- rollback_criteria: when to revert a deploy or config change
- post_action_tasks: TODOs after mitigation (postmortem, incident review kickoff)

Example quick mitigation snippet (bash)
```
# check pod health
kubectl get pods -n runtime | grep runtime-api
# tail logs from one pod
kubectl logs -n runtime runtime-api-abc123 -f
# scale down canary
kubectl -n runtime set image deployment/runtime-api runtime-api=registry.redwood-inference.com/runtime-api:v2027-04-12 --record
```

Runbook quality checklist (automated review)
- < 6 steps in quick mitigation section
- copy-paste runnable commands
- clear ownership fields and contact methods
- links to related metrics and dashboards

4) Incident Review and Postmortem Standards

When incident severity meets the threshold (SEV2+ or when error budget exhausted), teams must produce a postmortem within 72 hours. Postmortem structure: summary, timeline, detection, impact, root cause analysis (RCA), corrective actions (owners + deadlines), lessons learned, and link to follow-up tickets.

Minimum incident metadata
- incident_id (YYYYMMDD-XXX)
- severity (SEV1/SEV2/SEV3)
- start_time, end_time (ISO 8601)
- affected_services list
- customer_impact_description
- immediate_actions_taken

Postmortem policy
1. Draft due: 72 hours after incident declared resolved.
2. Public exec summary due: 5 business days for SEV1/SEV2.
3. Root cause follow-up tickets created and assigned within 7 days.
4. Closed loop: verify remediation effectiveness within 30 days and update SLOs/capacity if necessary.

5) Reliability Initiative Framework

Definition: reliability initiatives are time-boxed, measurable projects aimed at reducing SLO burn or improving recovery time. Each initiative must have a clear KPI (SLO improvement, MTTR reduction, cost per 1k tokens improvement).

Initiative template
- initiative_name
- owner (team + PM)
- goal and KPI (quantitative target)
- timeline and milestones
- success criteria and measurement (how metrics will be computed)
- risks and mitigating actions

Examples
- KV-cache partitioning (eng-serving-runtime): reduce tail latency p99 by 20% for long-sequence workloads in EU region in 90 days.
- Billing pipeline resilience (eng-infra): reduce data loss incidents to 0 in 6 months via idempotent reprocessing.

6) Operational Tooling and Dashboards

Dashboard standards
- One primary SLO dashboard per service showing SLI, SLO, error budget burn rate, and top correlated metrics.
- One oncall runbook dashboard with quick links to runbooks, key logs, and live traces.
- Cost+usage dashboard for services with material billing exposure (>$2k/month).

Alerting standards
- Alerts must be actionable with a documented runbook link.
- Avoid alert fatigue: prefer multi-window detection (e.g., 1m for oncall, 15m for paging) and composite signals where appropriate.
- Annotate alerts with suppression windows for deploys and maintenance.

Tooling integrations (required)
- Metrics: Prometheus/Datadog (link to canonical metric)
- Tracing: OpenTelemetry/Jaeger (trace sampling policy)
- Logs: ELK/CloudLogging (retention policy link)
- Oncall: PagerDuty (rotation and escalation policy)

7) Ownership, Review Cadence, and Documentation Governance

- Ownership: Each SLO, capacity plan, runbook, and incident postmortem must have a named owner (team + person). The owner is responsible for maintenance and quarterly reviews.
- Review cadence: Quarterly SLO and capacity review with SRE leads. Reliability initiatives are reviewed monthly in the Reliability Council.
- Documentation governance: All SRE docs must live in Confluence under eng-sre. Use the SRE doc template (link) and include metadata fields. Docs older than 12 months require owner re-affirmation or archival.

Appendix A: SLO YAML example (for reference)
```
name: runtime-api-availability
description: successful responses to client generate requests
sli:
  query: "sum(rate(requests_success_total{service=\"runtime-api\"}[5m])) / sum(rate(requests_total{service=\"runtime-api\"}[5m]))"
objective: 0.9995
window: 30d
owner: eng-serving-runtime-oncall@redwood.com
error_budget_policy:
  low_threshold: 0.25
  medium_threshold: 0.50
  actions:
    - medium: notify-sre-lead, begin capacity assessment
    - high: freeze-rollouts, auto-scale, exec-notify
```

Appendix B: SLO Review Template (Quarterly)
1. Current SLO attainment and trend (30d, 90d).
2. Error budget burn rate and root causes of any major burns.
3. Capacity headroom and upcoming events that may affect traffic.
4. Planned reliability initiatives and owner status.
5. Outstanding runbooks and missing quick-checks.
